reviews.summary:
Reviewer David questioned the necessity of a specific check in follow_page_mask(), asking why it's required and whether trying to fill non-existent pages is beneficial.

Reviewer David suggested reusing the 'page' variable instead of introducing a new subpage concept, pointing out that Willy's repeated mention of it is incorrect.

Reviewer David suggested basing the patch on the GUP-fast batching series, using its helper by passing vma=NULL, and questioned why GUP-fast doesn't require similar optimizations.
reviews.raw_body:
Why is that check needed? Why should someone try filling something that doesn't
exist?

---

There is no such thing as a subpage as Willy keeps saying :)

Why not reuse "page" ?

	for (i = 0; i < nr; i++, page++) {

---

Now I wonder why GUP-fast doesn't need any of that. Likely because architectures
that support GUP-fast don't need any such magic.

Maybe we should in fact base this on the gup-fast batching series and also use
the helper in there (passing vma=NULL)?

-- 
Cheers,

David

reviews.author: Rik Riel (author)
reviews.summary:
The author acknowledged that faultin_page_range() and populate_vma_page_range both call the GUP code with a NULL pages pointer, indicating that these paths need to be updated to handle this case.

The author is addressing David's concern that the dcache flush in slow GUP is not necessary for most callers, but rather only a few oddball cases need it. The author explains that this asymmetry can be solved by either adding dcache flushing to unpin_user_pages_dirty_lock() or moving the cache flushing to the GUP callers. However, the author notes that KSM uses GUP and would like to see the latest page contents.

Author acknowledged that the batch filling of pages can be done inline in a helper and asked for clarification on which batching series is being referred to, indicating a potential reevaluation of the code structure.
reviews.raw_body:
faultin_page_range() and populate_vma_page_range
both call the GUP code with a NULL pages pointer.

---

These cache flushes seem to be common on architectures
with virtually indexed caches, where the cache needs 
to be flushed if the memory is accessed through a 
different virtual address than where userspace might
have written data.

On 32 bit ARM, MIPS, and sh, the kernel seems to
implement an actual cache flush here, but also
claims to support GUP-fast.

I don't understand how that would possibly be safe,
since the pages returned by GUP-fast could be
accessed under a different cache alias than where
userspace accesses the memory.

I think one reason GUP-fast can get away without
a dcache flush is that most of the callers take
care of that, for example by using raw_copy_to_user()
to copy data using the user's virtual address, which
takes care of VIVT cache aliasing.

Likewise, drivers that do zero-copy DMA into user
memory will get the cache flushed on VIVT architectures
inside dma_unmap().

The dcache flush inside GUP covers rarer cases, where
the kernel accesses memory at a different address than
where userspace wrote to that memory.

 cat /proc/<pid>/cmdline              KERNEL
 ----                                 -------------------
 read(buf=U)
   -------------------------------->
                                      get_mm_cmdline(mm, U):
                                        access_remote_vm(mm, arg_start,
                                          kbuf, len, FOLL_ANON):
                                          get_user_page_vma_remote()
                                          (slow GUP + its flushes)
                                          kmap_local_folio(P)
                                          memcpy(kbuf <- K)   // read
                                          kunmap_local(K)
                                        copy_to_user(U, kbuf) // write
                                          through U itself
 read buf at U
   ------>
            clean: the final write to U went
            through U. Same line. No hazard.

In this case, the dcache flush in slow GUP ensures
that data written before the GUP is visible to the
reader.

In the write path, e.g. for PTRACE_POKE, __access_remote_vm
flushes after the write has been done, so the other
process will see the data on the next read.

It looks like process_vm_writev() might be missing that
cache flush after a write, though.

However, now we have a situation where:
1) Only a few oddball callers of GUP need the dcache flush, and
2) Those need to do their OWN flush after a write, and
3) The dcache flush is not needed for most other GUP callers.

We could do two different things here to solve the
asymmetry.

Either we could add dcache flushing to 
unpin_user_pages_dirty_lock(), and make sure all
the callers that need to call that function, or
we could move the cache flushing to the GUP callers.

Then we have KSM, which uses GUP, and which would like
to see the latest page contents...

---

I just moved this code out of __get_user_pages(),
but if we can get rid of it completely by using
a different helper, all the better.

Which GUP-fast batching series are you talking
about, here?

In Yeoreum Yun's series, the batch filling seems 
to be done inline in gup_fast_pte_range(), and not
in a helper:

https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261102-refactor_gup_fast-v2-4-bc1ac018c834@arm.com/

Should both paths be using the same gup_fill_pages()
helper?

The cache flushing part is broken out into its own
helper function later in this series, so we could
sequence those differently.

-- 
All Rights Reversed.

reviews.author: David (Arm)
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David pointed out that the patch's code change was unnecessary because it assumed a GUP user without a pages array, which is not the case.

Reviewer David (Arm) expressed concerns about the inconsistency, lack of documentation, and potential errors in the GUP-fast implementation, specifically questioning whether the dcache should be flushed when using this path or if it must always be done under the PT lock.

Reviewer David suggested that instead of manually looping, all functions should use a helper to fill an array, and proposed distinguishing between gup and gup-fast using the VMA argument.
reviews.raw_body:
That's not what I meant. I know that we have GUP users without
pages array.

In the code change you are performing the check is not required.

That's why there wasn't one in the first place.

---

It's all very inconsistent. And undocumented. And error prone.

Could we have GUP-fast also flush the dcache for consistency or
must that only be called with the PT lock held?

---

We also have gup_fast_pmd_leaf that fills an array. I think all of these should
just use a helper (instead of manually looping).

For now we can distinguish gup vs. gup-fast using the VMA argument.

-- 
Cheers,

David

reviews.author: Rik Riel (author)
reviews.summary:
Author is considering simplifying the code by removing a dependency on the caller to check if pages exist, instead adding the check directly into the gup_fill_pages() function.

The author is addressing a concern about dcache flushes in gup_fast callers, explaining that many drivers already handle their own flushing and only a small number of slow GUP callers need dcache flushes. The author suggests moving the cache flushes out of follow_page_mask() into __get_user_pages(), which may allow for merging helper functions between slow and fast GUP.

Author agrees that the new helpers can be unified and plans to make this change in a future version, but does not provide a specific plan for when or how it will be done.
reviews.raw_body:
It looks like 2 of the 3 callers of gup_fill_pages()
check for pages existing. The other does not.

Should we just have the check in this one place, and
not depend on the caller?

---

I think we could, but it does not look like any of
them need it.

Out of the 83 callers of gup_fast, many DMA into the
page, and the drivers do their own flushing. Also,
flushing before the DMA write doesn't help.

KVM, Infiniband, and others pin the pages, sometimes
for longer periods of time, and either flush around 
their reads and writes, or run only on architectures
where we don't need to.

The others access the page through the user's own
virtual address, which again does not require a
dcache flush.

Only a small number of slow GUP callers need dcache
flushes.

It may make more sense to move the cache flushes
all the way out into __get_user_pages() and away
from the follow_page_mask() call chain, so we can
maybe merge more of the helper functions between
slow GUP and fast GUP.

---

I think all of those could use the same helper
function I am breaking out here, once the dcache
flushing moves to its own helper.

-- 
All Rights Reversed.

reviews.raw_body:
That should be spelled out in the patch description.

The change as it stands in this patch looks useless :)

Although trying to fill something that doesn't exist is a bit weird.

But if it makes the calling code nicer, sure.

reviews.author: Rik Riel (author)
reviews.summary:
Author agreed that patch 7 by itself isn't super useful but plans to restructure it in v2 to move cache flushing out from under the lock, allowing GUP-fast and regular GUP to share the same helper.

Author is addressing a concern about cache flushing in GUP callers, proposing to either fold the changes into the existing series or send them as a separate prequel series. The proposed solution involves moving the cache flush calls up the stack into pin_user_pages_remote() and get_user_pages_remote().
reviews.raw_body:
I agree this patch by itself isn't super useful.

It's goal is to be able to have this code in one
spot, and not in multiple places in gup.c

I'll split out the array filling from the cache
flushing, so we can move the cache flushing out
from under the lock, and have GUP-fast and regular
GUP share the same helper.

---

It really doesn't look too bad. Here are all
the GUP callers that need a cache flush:
- kernel/events/uprobes.c (through get_user_pages_remote)
- /proc/pid/cmdline (through access_remote_vm)
- fs/proc/base.c (through access_remote_vm)
- kernel/trace/trace_events_user.c (pin_user_pages_remote)
- arch/x86/kernel/cpu/sgx/ioctl.c (get_user_pages ... urgh)
- kernel/ptrace.c (access_remote_vm)
- mm/process_vm_access.c (pin_user_pages_remote)
- fs/exec.c (pin_user_pages_remote)
- virt/kvm/async_pf.c (get_user_pages_remote)

In other words, if we change the SGX code to just
call get_user_pages_remote(), and then move the
cache flushing to get_user_pages_remote() and
pin_user_pages_remote() we should be all set.

Want me to fold that into this series, or send
it in as a small, separate prequel series?

As a separate series it would:
1) split out the gup_fill_pages() and gup_flush_pages()
   helpers
2) convert the SGX code to use get_user_pages_remote()
3) move the flush call up the stack into pin_user_pages_remote()
   and get_user_pages_remote()

Just let me know if you prefer that separate, or
folded in. 

-- 
All Rights Reversed.

reviews.author: Rik Riel (author)
reviews.summary:
Author acknowledged that the patch's performance benefits are not as significant for small pages and agreed to re-evaluate the approach, indicating a potential need for further revision.

Author agrees to fold David's suggested cleanup into their series or send it separately, indicating a willingness to incorporate feedback and potentially revise the patch.
reviews.raw_body:
On Tue, 3 Nov 2026 17:55:31 +0100
"David Hildenbrand (Arm)" <david@kernel.org> wrote:

---

That sounds good. It looks like with this small change below,
GUP-fast and slow GUP can share another helper.

I can fold that into my series as well, or send the cleanups
in a separate series, whatever works best for you.

The PUD and PMD paths do not look as easy to untangle, but
maybe after some more cleanups on each end?

---8<---

diff --git a/mm/gup.c b/mm/gup.c
--- a/mm/gup.c
+++ b/mm/gup.c
@@ -940,14 +940,20 @@
  * run under FOLL_WRITE or FOLL_PIN does need the per-page check, so it stays
  * one page at a time.
+ *
+ * @fpb_flags selects the scan: slow GUP merges young/dirty so
+ * folio_mark_dirty() sees any dirty PTE in the run; fast GUP scans
+ * locklessly and revalidates the run after grabbing it. @vma is only
+ * needed for FPB_MERGE_WRITE and may be NULL otherwise.
  */
 static unsigned long gup_pte_batch_len(struct vm_area_struct *vma,
 		unsigned long address, unsigned long walk_end,
-		struct folio *folio, pte_t *ptep, pte_t *batch_pte, unsigned int flags)
+		struct folio *folio, pte_t *ptep, pte_t *batch_pte,
+		unsigned int flags, fpb_t fpb_flags)
 {
 	unsigned long max;
@@ -961,8 +961,7 @@
 	max = (walk_end - address) >> PAGE_SHIFT;
 	if (max <= 1)
 		return 1;
 
-	/* Merge young/dirty across batch so folio_mark_dirty sees any dirty. */
 	return folio_pte_batch_flags(folio, vma, ptep, batch_pte, max,
-				     FPB_RESPECT_WRITE | FPB_MERGE_YOUNG_DIRTY);
+				     fpb_flags);
 }
@@ -1018,7 +1018,8 @@
 			folio = page_folio(page);
 			batch_pte = pte;
 
 			batch = gup_pte_batch_len(vma, address, walk_end, folio,
-					 ptep, &batch_pte, flags);
+					 ptep, &batch_pte, flags,
+					 FPB_RESPECT_WRITE | FPB_MERGE_YOUNG_DIRTY);
 			ret = gup_grab_folio_pages(folio, page, batch,
 						     pte_dirty(batch_pte), flags,

2026-11-03.patch_summary: This patch series optimizes the follow_page_mask() function by allowing it to return a batch of pages instead of walking the page tables one page at a time. This is achieved through a series of changes, including moving helper functions into separate files and splitting the work of grabbing folio references and storing pages from the original function. The patches also introduce new helpers for looking up PTEs in batches and reporting huge page subpage counts. The result is improved performance, with benchmarks showing a 2.3x improvement on base pages and a 5.9x improvement on large mTHP folios.
